source_title: Jordan says its air force undertook strikes against militant hideouts in Syria News - World | October 26
source_excerpt:
Strikes followed earlier announcement that 3 suspects arrested in recent church attack
Jordan said Monday that its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
The armed ​forces said the operation was conducted in co-ordination with Damascus. Syria's government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security co-ordination in ​border areas.
Damascus informed Jordan of its "complete reservation" over the strikes without prior co-ordination, the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Seven people, including three ​children and a woman, were killed and three others were wounded in the Jordanian strikes, the Syrian Civil Defence ⁠said in a preliminary report. ⁠It said emergency teams responded to four sites hit by the strikes ‌in the countryside of Daraa and Sweida provinces.
Jordan did not immediately comment on that account.
A building shows signs of gunfire at the site where Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects in connection with Friday's shooting. (Alaa Al Sukhni/Reuters)
Shortly after the strikes, Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, citing developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.
Nassib is ⁠Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.
Earlier on Monday, senior ⁠government security officials said Jordanian ⁠security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday over the church violence that ​killed nine people.
"God willing, they only represent themselves," said Maj.-Gen. Obeidallah al-Maaytah, Jordan's director of public security.
Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable U.S. ally in the Middle East. Friday's attack on the Christian ⁠minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist."
In a press conference, al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism.
"The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications ⁠of any links between them and other cells," al-Faraya added.
Friday's attack during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, in Karak governorate, about 120 kilometres southwest of the capital of Amman, also wounded at least ​34 people. Witnesses said gunmen opened fire for several minutes. The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. The three ⁠suspects were named in the press briefing.
Reuters video footage showed a building pockmarked by the exchange of ⁠fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate.
Mourners gather around a grave as the flag-draped coffin of a victim killed in an attack on a Greek Orthodox church is lowered for burial during a funeral in Karak, Jordan, on Sunday. (Raad Adayleh/The Associated Press)
Jordan's Public Security Directorate in a statement carried ⁠by ⁠state media said that security forces located the ​suspects while they were hiding in an abandoned house. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them.
No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects' possession.
There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack.
Jordan, a U.S. partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past. The security officials did not name any Islamist groups ⁠in the press conference.
